title: Testing the Website with People Who Use It Differently
script: Narrator: [reflective] Our volunteer team thought the new website was ready because it looked clean on our laptops and the registration form worked during our own tests.

Narrator: Then a visitor using a screen reader tried to register for an event. Several buttons had no useful labels, the form did not explain errors clearly, and the confirmation message was difficult to reach.
Narrator: The experience changed our idea of testing. We had checked whether the site worked for people who built it. We had not checked whether it worked for the range of people expected to use it.
Narrator: We invited feedback from users with different access needs and paid attention to what happened in practice rather than defending what we intended a feature to do.

Narrator: The repairs were not mysterious: clear headings, readable contrast, keyboard access, descriptive labels, captions where needed, and a contact route that did not require someone to describe their private situation publicly.

Narrator: We also learned not to treat one tester as a spokesperson for everyone. Accessibility includes many different experiences, and people should not have to volunteer their time endlessly to prove that a service is inclusive.

Narrator: The launch moved back by two weeks. At first, the delay felt frustrating. Later, we recognised that rushing had been easy only because some users would have carried the extra work of navigating our mistakes.
Narrator: This is why design has an ethical side. Exclusion can be produced by a missing label, an uncaptioned video, or a support process that assumes every person can call at the same time of day.
Narrator: The website improved because criticism was treated as useful evidence. That is a lesson for any system: people affected by a design often notice its limits first.

quiz.question: What exposed the weakness in the team's original test process?
options: The site used too many headings.
A screen-reader user could not complete important parts of registration.
The team tested after the public launch.
A visitor asked for an event cancellation.
quiz.explanation: The visitor found unlabeled buttons, unclear errors, and a hard-to-reach confirmation.

quiz.question: How did the experience revise the speaker's definition of successful testing?
options: A team should test only the features it built itself.
A clean layout proves broad usability.
Testing must include the different people expected to use the service.
Technical teams should avoid asking visitors for feedback.
quiz.explanation: The original testing worked for builders but not the range of intended users.

quiz.question: Why does the narrator stress observing what happens in practice?
options: Intended design can differ from users' actual experience.
Users should not be told how a site works.
Feedback matters only after a complete redesign.
A design team cannot understand accessibility.
quiz.explanation: The speaker contrasts the team's intention with the barriers users actually encountered.

quiz.question: Which repair best reflects the speaker's concern for privacy as well as access?
options: Requiring callers to explain their circumstances to get help
Using one tester's account as the complete accessibility standard
Replacing captions with a longer privacy policy
Offering a contact route that avoids public disclosure of private needs
quiz.explanation: The proposed contact route should not force people to reveal personal circumstances publicly.

quiz.question: What does the warning about one tester prevent?
options: Treating personal testimony as unimportant
Treating one person's experience as representative of every access need
Delaying all changes until every issue is identical
Giving users a way to report problems
quiz.explanation: The speaker values feedback while recognising that accessibility includes diverse experiences.

quiz.question: Why did the launch delay later seem more justifiable to the narrator?
options: The delay allowed the team to remove all support options.
It made the site look more impressive on laptops.
Rushing would have transferred navigation work onto excluded users.
The visitor had asked for the event to be cancelled.
quiz.explanation: The delay became an ethical issue once the team saw who would otherwise carry the burden.

quiz.question: What is the role of the examples of missing labels and uncaptioned video?
options: They show that exclusion can arise through small design and support choices.
They prove all websites should use the same layout.
They show that accessibility concerns only visual design.
They justify postponing feedback until after launch.
quiz.explanation: The narrator uses them to show that seemingly minor choices can create barriers.

quiz.question: Which inference follows from treating criticism as useful evidence?
options: Affected users can reveal limitations that designers fail to notice.
Criticism should be accepted only when it is polite.
Designers have no responsibility once a form submits.
Each feature needs approval from only one user.
quiz.explanation: The conclusion says people affected by a system often perceive its limits first.

quiz.question: Which proposal most conflicts with the narrator's reasoning?
options: Test keyboard navigation before public release.
Use descriptive labels for form controls.
Ask users with varied access needs about their experience.
Launch on schedule because internal laptop tests were successful.
quiz.explanation: The whole account challenges reliance on the team's own successful laptop testing.

quiz.question: What larger standard does the narrator apply to inclusive design?
options: A site is inclusive when its visual style is simple.
A service should work in practice for diverse users, not merely match designers' intentions.
Accessibility is complete once one barrier is repaired.
Support should use one communication method for everyone.
quiz.explanation: The narrator measures inclusion by actual use across different needs.
